title: Build a Complete CSS Website
subtitle: Bring Everything Together
description: Complete the CSS course by designing and building a professional responsive website from scratch. Apply selectors, colors, backgrounds, borders, box model, typography, Flexbox, Grid, responsive design, positioning, variables, pseudo-classes, transitions and animations. Finish with a critical assessment covering the most important concepts from Lessons 1 through 10.

blocks.text: Welcome to Your Final CSS Project
This is the final lesson of the CSS course.
We are not going to spend this lesson memorizing another long list of CSS properties.
We are going to build.
Your job is to think like a developer who has received a website design and needs to turn it into a working interface.
We will build a responsive learning-platform landing page.
The project will contain a navigation bar, hero section, course cards, statistics, call-to-action section and footer.
You will combine the CSS knowledge from the entire course.
Open your editor and create a folder for this project.
Inside it, create index.html and style.css.
Step 1: Build the HTML Structure
Remember the relationship between HTML and CSS.
HTML gives the page its structure.
CSS will control how that structure looks, behaves and adapts to different screens.
Start with this clean semantic structure.

blocks.text: Step 2: Create the Design System
Before styling individual components, create the visual foundation.
This is where CSS variables become extremely useful.
Instead of repeating the same colors everywhere, create reusable variables.

blocks.title: CSS Foundation
blocks.output: The page now has a reusable color system, predictable box sizing, responsive container and basic browser-safe foundations.

blocks.text: This small foundation will control a large part of the website.
Notice how one variable can be changed later and every component using it can update.
That is the beginning of thinking like a developer rather than styling each element randomly.
Step 3: Style the Navigation
Let's build the top navigation.
Flexbox is a natural choice because the navigation needs elements arranged along one direction.

blocks.title: Navigation
blocks.output: A sticky navigation bar with Flexbox alignment, reusable buttons and accessible hover/focus states.

blocks.text: We have already used several concepts from earlier lessons.
Flexbox controls the layout.
The box model controls spacing.
Positioning creates the sticky header.
Transitions make the navigation interaction smoother.
Step 4: Build the Hero
The hero is the first major section users see.
We want strong typography, useful spacing and a clear visual hierarchy.

blocks.title: Hero Section
blocks.output: A responsive hero area with a strong heading, call-to-action buttons and course progress card.

blocks.text: Notice the use of clamp for responsive typography and spacing.
The hero is already designed to adapt instead of relying entirely on fixed sizes.
Step 5: Build the Course Grid
Now we need several course cards arranged in a responsive grid.
This is where CSS Grid becomes especially useful.

blocks.title: Course Cards
blocks.output: Three course cards arranged with CSS Grid and enhanced using a subtle hover transition.

blocks.text: The grid creates the large-screen structure.
The cards themselves use the box model, borders, colors, transitions and transforms.
Step 6: Statistics and CTA
A complete website needs visual rhythm between sections.

blocks.title: Stats and CTA
blocks.output: A statistics section and final call-to-action block.

blocks.text: Step 7: Finish the Footer

blocks.title: Footer
blocks.output: A simple footer completes the page structure.

blocks.text: The website now has its main visual structure.
But we are not finished.
A website that only looks good on a large screen is not a finished responsive website.
Step 8: Make It Responsive
Now test your website on a narrow screen.
You will probably notice that the two-column hero and three-column course grid need to change.
This is exactly why we learned media queries.

blocks.title: Responsive Layout
blocks.output: The layout changes from three columns to two and finally to one column as the screen becomes smaller.

blocks.text: Run the page on your phone.
Resize the browser if possible.
Look for horizontal scrolling, cramped text, overflowing buttons and cards that become too narrow.
Responsive development is not finished until you test the actual interface.
Step 9: Add Purposeful Motion
Our final website should feel alive, but we do not want unnecessary movement everywhere.

blocks.title: Entrance Animation
blocks.output: The hero enters smoothly and buttons receive subtle interactive motion.

blocks.text: This is enough motion to make the interface feel polished.
We do not need to make every card spin, bounce or continuously move.
Remember what you learned in Lesson 9: animation should have a purpose.
Step 10: Final Developer Inspection
Before calling the project complete, inspect it like a professional developer.
Check the HTML structure.
Check your selectors.
Check spacing and box sizing.
Check typography.
Check Grid and Flexbox.
Check mobile responsiveness.
Check hover and keyboard focus.
Check animations.
Finally, check whether the interface actually communicates what it is supposed to communicate.
That final question is more important than whether you remember every CSS property.
Critical Assessment: Lessons 1–10
Now comes your final CSS assessment.
These questions are deliberately close.
Several answers may look correct at first.
Choose the solution that best matches the actual developer requirement.

blocks.question: You have three different buttons that should all use the same blue background, rounded corners and padding. Which CSS approach is the most maintainable?
options: Give every button a different ID and repeat the same declarations
Create one reusable class and apply it to all three buttons
Use an element selector that affects every element on the page
Write the same CSS directly inside each HTML button
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A reusable class is the best fit when several components share the same visual role.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about maintainability. If the blue changes later, which solution lets you update all three buttons in one place?
blocks.reasoning: Lesson 2 introduced classes as reusable selectors. A shared class allows several elements to receive the same styling without repeating CSS.
blocks.hint: You have three elements with the same design role. Which selector is designed for reuse?

blocks.question: A card has width: 300px, padding: 20px on both sides and a 2px border on both sides. With the default box-sizing: content-box, what is the card's outer width?
options: 300px because width defines the complete card
340px because padding is added but borders are included
344px because content, padding and borders all contribute
344px only when box-sizing is border-box
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. With content-box, the declared 300px is the content width, so 40px of horizontal padding and 4px of horizontal borders are added.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember the Box Model. With content-box, declared width describes the content area, not the entire outer box.
blocks.reasoning: 300px content + 20px left padding + 20px right padding + 2px left border + 2px right border = 344px outer width.
blocks.hint: Calculate content + left padding + right padding + left border + right border.

blocks.question: A desktop layout has a navigation row, a large hero section and three equal course cards. Which combination best matches the layout requirements?
options: Flexbox for everything because every layout should use one system
Grid for the three-card structure and Flexbox for one-dimensional alignment
Grid only for the navigation and absolute positioning for the cards
Absolute positioning for the hero and Flexbox only for the footer
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Grid is excellent for the two-dimensional card structure, while Flexbox is ideal for one-dimensional rows such as navigation.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Do not choose a layout system simply because it can technically create the result. Match the tool to the structure.
blocks.reasoning: Lesson 6 and Lesson 7 taught that Flexbox excels at one-dimensional alignment while Grid handles structured rows and columns.
blocks.hint: Ask whether each part is mainly one-dimensional or a row-and-column structure.

blocks.question: A website looks correct on a 1200px screen, but on a 360px phone the course cards become too narrow and the page develops horizontal overflow. Which fix is most appropriate?
options: Increase the card width so the content has more room
Keep the desktop three-column grid and reduce only the font size
Use a responsive media query to change the grid to fewer columns and ensure children can shrink
Set the entire body to width: 1200px so the desktop layout remains unchanged
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Responsive layout means changing the structure when the available space becomes insufficient.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The problem is not simply font size. The layout itself is demanding more horizontal space than the phone provides.
blocks.reasoning: Responsive design uses media queries and flexible sizing to adapt the layout. A three-column desktop grid commonly becomes two or one column on smaller screens.
blocks.hint: The screen is too narrow for the current structure. Change the structure rather than forcing the phone to behave like a desktop.

blocks.question: A navigation bar should remain visible near the top while the user scrolls, but it should still occupy its normal place in the page layout. Which positioning choice best fits this requirement?
options: position: absolute
position: fixed
position: sticky
position: relative with a very large z-index
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Sticky positioning allows an element to behave normally until it reaches its threshold, then remain attached within its scrolling context.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The requirement says the element should remain part of the normal layout before sticking.
blocks.reasoning: Fixed positioning removes the element from normal document flow and attaches it to the viewport. Sticky combines normal-flow behavior with a sticking threshold.
blocks.hint: Which positioning mode behaves normally first and then sticks?

blocks.question: A designer wants a heading to remain readable across phones, tablets and desktop without creating several separate font-size rules. Which approach best matches the requirement?
options: Use one very large fixed font-size for every screen
Use clamp() with a minimum, flexible preferred value and maximum
Use only vw and allow the font to grow without limits
Use different IDs for the heading at each screen size
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. clamp() gives the value a minimum, a flexible preferred size and a maximum.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The requirement asks for controlled flexibility, not unlimited scaling.
blocks.reasoning: Responsive typography should remain readable at small sizes while still growing on larger screens. clamp() provides those boundaries.
blocks.hint: Which CSS function gives you a minimum, preferred and maximum value?

blocks.question: A course card should lift slightly when hovered, while a notification should automatically slide into view when created. Which pairing is most appropriate?
options: Both should use transition because all motion is a transition
Card: transition with transform; notification: @keyframes animation
Card: @keyframes infinite; notification: transition on hover
Card: margin change; notification: position: fixed
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The card responds to a hover state, while the notification needs an independent entrance animation.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Separate state changes from animations that need to run independently.
blocks.reasoning: Lesson 9 established the key distinction: transition is ideal for state changes such as hover, while keyframes are useful for independent or multi-stage animations.

blocks.question: A developer wants every card on the website to use the same border radius, spacing system and main colors. Which approach best supports future maintenance?
options: Repeat the values inside every card rule so each card is independent
Use CSS variables for shared design values and reusable classes for shared components
Use inline styles because they are easier to find
Create a separate ID for every card and copy the same values
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Variables centralize design values while reusable classes centralize component behavior.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about what happens when the design changes later. You want one place to update shared values.
blocks.reasoning: CSS custom properties are ideal for design tokens such as colors, spacing and radius. Classes handle reusable component styling.
blocks.hint: What would make changing the entire site's primary color take one edit?

blocks.question: You finish a responsive website. The layout works, but keyboard users cannot clearly see which navigation link has focus, and the page contains unnecessary continuous animations. What is the best final improvement?
options: Remove all hover effects and increase every animation
Add clear :focus-visible states and reduce unnecessary motion, including respecting prefers-reduced-motion
Replace Flexbox with Grid and remove the media queries
Increase z-index values and make every animation infinite
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent. This combines two important professional concerns: keyboard accessibility and responsible motion.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The problems are accessibility and unnecessary motion, not layout or stacking.
blocks.reasoning: A finished website must work for more than mouse users. :focus-visible provides a clear keyboard focus state, while prefers-reduced-motion lets users request less motion.
blocks.hint: Which answer addresses both the keyboard problem and the animation problem directly?

blocks.text: What You Have Actually Learned
You started this course by learning that CSS controls the presentation of HTML.
But that definition is no longer enough for you.
You can now reason about selectors.
You can control color, backgrounds, borders and visual identity.
You understand the Box Model and can diagnose spacing problems.
You can create readable typography.
You can arrange real interfaces with Flexbox and Grid.
You can make those interfaces respond to different screen sizes.
You can control positioning, layering and reusable design variables.
You can create interaction with pseudo-classes.
You can create visual details with pseudo-elements.
You can create purposeful transitions and animations.
Most importantly, you can combine these tools to build an actual website.
The Bigger Goal
Do not stop at this project.
The purpose of this course was never to make you memorize CSS properties.
The purpose was to teach you how to turn an idea or design into a working interface.
You can now take the same thinking and create landing pages, dashboards, portfolios, learning platforms, forms, product pages and application interfaces.
Later, JavaScript will give those interfaces behavior and logic.
React will later help you organize large interactive interfaces into reusable components.
Your goal is not to become someone who can only write CSS.
Your goal is to become someone who can look at a problem and build the interface needed to solve it.
That is the developer mindset.
CSS Course Complete
Congratulations.
You have completed the CSS course.
You have moved from basic styling to building complete responsive interfaces.
Save your final project.
Open it on your phone.
Test every section.
Then ask yourself one final question.
What can I build next?
That question is where your real development journey begins.
